text:
Fair question!

I still stand by that article.  Code that doesn't (need to) exist is preferable to code that was generated.

For a lot of glue code, I think I have an answer with Objective-Smalltalk.

But there is a lot of tedious code out there that I don't have an answer for.  Yet. :-) And not all of it is necessarily glue code.  And you also need to bring the existing sprawl into the brave new world of polymorphic architectural abstraction.

One example:  as one application of Objective-Smalltalk, I've been working on an "across-native" UI framework I call InterScript.  The idea is to have as rich a model as possible to then hook up to UIs that are as thin as possible, either native AppKit, UIKit, Android or HTMX/HTMXNative.  And have a (customizable) default UI generated for you a la naked objects or WebObjects Direct2Web.

So to get a table-view with some data, just create the table and "write" it to the UI generator (bound to the guy variable).

table ← #MPWDictArrayTable[
  #{ first: "Marcel", last: "Weiher" },
  #{ first: "Peter", last: "Alexander"},
  #{ first: "Hello", last: "World"},
  #{ first: "Hi", last: "There"}
].

gui ! table.


Now that's nice and concise, but it takes a good amount of code to get there.  Most of that code is not particularly exciting, and the idea of writing this code for AppKit, UIKit, Android and HTMX was...daunting to the point of not really being feasible for me, at least not with other things I also need to do.  Claude and to a lesser extent Codex helped me quite a bit here, and without that assistance I might never have embarked on the journey.   I give it UI to generate, then adapt it to the structure I need, though it's been getting better at figuring that out.

Similar with code-generation.  One example was that I early on had to make a choice as to whether to transpile to Objective-C or generate native code directly.  There are good reasons for both approaches. I decided to go with direct native, with good results.  Recently, I have decided to follow the Objective-C transpilation fork as well, because the effort required to do so is low enough that I can let that run on-the-side.  And also pursue an Objective-J transpiler to see if I can use Cappuccino to get some AppKit-like UI components for the Web (browsers, table-views).

Another example:  I am far from an expert on object-files and linkers, but the way of generating data in object-files seemed extremely manual, tedious and brittle to me.  I thought that at least for objects, I should be able to create a Mach-O serializer:  just write the object to the serializer and it places an appropriate binary representation in the Mach-O, with the data filled where needed and relocation entries/symbol entries for the pointers.

A lot of moving parts and my understanding of the subject matter is limited.  I had an AI generate the first version.  Despite me saying what I wanted, that version actually hard-coded generation for the initial data structures I had given as examples. It was also structurally wrong in a couple of places.  But it reduced the cognitive load enough for me to refactor that to what I wanted under the auspices of the tests.

So that's how AI generation has been liberating:  it allows me to tackle problems that would otherwise be too big, too daunting, or maybe seem too daunting. It gives me a first cut of something that I can refine and condense.  It allows me to have fewer context-switches between creating and critiquing.

So far there hasn't really been duplicated boiler-plate code that shouldn't exist.

Coding tools have gotten more powerful.  We can use that power to make it easier for us to produce slop, or we can set our sights higher, realizing that things that used to be firmly out of our reach might no longer be.

Per aspera ad astra.

Perhaps the ubiquity of LLMs is indeed not the right target of blame here, true: in a different world, with different incentives around software engineering, and indeed economics and society at large, LLMs might have been taken up and used differently. Might have; I honestly kind of doubt that. It is true that the overblown state of the big AI companies fits well with how our (Western) economy works, but they would have been invented and developed regardless. Possibly more slowly.

However, our economy does not spring from a void; humans are susceptible to power. Not everyone is, but enough are, and enough are willing to follow someone with power, that these kind of structures have a strong tendency to form. And the point of the OP seems to be majorly that "AI chat was making [them] delusional." We have plenty of reports of this happening to people, even though it happens to far from everyone. And again, it's human nature: LLMs write in a way that exploits our internal heuristics for believability of information, which depend fairly significantly on how well the information is presented. (Others have already written about this.) Of course we can't be certain if LLMs would have had the same effect on society had they been introduced more slowly, and in a society less consumed by monetary greed, but I think we'd start seeing similar effects -- just more slowly.

All that is to say: if we can't blame AI for this, can we really blame society? Should we instead blame ourselves, perhaps, or how our brains work? That's hardly productive, unless you consider it productive to conclude that the human race had better not exist. (Which is, by the way, a point of view I find very difficult to refute.) So in absence of a good root cause to usefully blame, I think it's not so bad to blame AI, or at least the companies driving AI: if we can't fix the root cause, we'd better work around the worst outcroppings of our natures, and instead of doing that we seem to be diving headlong into the deep.

I think it's defensible to have a crisis about that.

Exactly. I shared /s/hhtuqh some time back where I argued that there are a few principles we should consistently follow when talking about AI in general (which apply just as well to LLMs in particular). To summarise them:


Do not anthropomorphise AI systems.

Do not blindly trust the output of AI systems.

Retain full human responsibility and accountability for any consequences arising from the use of AI systems.


I try to stick to these guidelines when I talk about LLMs myself. For example, I deliberately say 'I queried ChatGPT' rather than 'I asked ChatGPT'. Similarly, I say 'The output from Claude indicates' or 'Claude produced' instead of 'Claude said'.

I would like to see the language around AI become less anthropomorphic and more technical, because I believe that precise language encourages clearer thinking and better judgement.

But alas, ideas like this do not travel very far when I express them on my little website. It would help if more prominent personalities articulated similar principles, so this way of speaking becomes more widely adopted.

A few possibly-disjointed thoughts:

Over the past year or so I read literally hundreds of pages' worth of studies and papers looking at the impact of LLM-assisted coding, and then a little while back I wrote up a multi-thousand-word blog post summarizing (among other things) what I saw in all that reading. A big takeaway was that while developers self-reported feeling more productive and producing more and better code, metrics like production incidents, CI pipeline breakage, and mean time to recovery were all trending in the bad direction. This lines up with the already-mentioned METR paper whose important conclusion was not necessarily "LLMs bad", but "developers are bad at self-estimating their productivity and the impact of tools on it".

The most common responses I got from LLM enthusiasts on that post were:


Insisting that the inflection point after which LLMs are asserted to be revolutionarily good must have occurred just after the data-gathering phase of any studies which found negative impacts, and

Insisting that I just must not have enough personal experience with LLM coding to be able to realize how great it is and how much it would boost my productivity.


I found this disappointing, to say the least. And trying to deflect to talking about lack of positive evidence for other practices, when for LLMs we have things like before-and-after measurements of failure rates and MTTR for millions of CI pipelines, is also disappointing.

Anyway. I do see a common thread that many of the people reporting the biggest impacts are people who do not do what I do. I work at a company, with a team of other developers and product people and other people, all collaborating to build and maintain software. Many of the people who are the biggest boosters and claiming the biggest impacts do not do this; they mostly work independently and solo or close to it. I'm willing to grant the possibility that there is something to a single highly-competent programmer making things to suit their own vision and preference, and that perhaps this is a case where LLMs do a lot better. But I have also seen the literature on adoption in larger teams, and I have worked on multiple such teams where people tried pushing LLM-assisted coding and I've seen exactly the kind of mixed impact the literature consistently reports.

And the ancedotal examples we have of companies going all-in do not present something to emulate. Microsoft went all-in and their flagship developer-facing property became a literal byword for unreliability right around the same time. Are those two things connected? Maybe not, but it certainly doesn't help the image of LLM coding.

The negatives are very very real and I'm getting tired of being told, directly or indirectly, not to believe what I've seen with my own eyes. I'm willing to grant that your experience is as you've described, and all I ask in return is that you grant me the same courtesy.

The impact of an agent on greenfield projects is dramatically different than the impact on brownfield projects. I’ve been out of the web standards space for a couple years now, so this is pure speculation on my part. But I imagine that a lot of the efforts to improve the ergonomics of building websites – better CSS shorthands, terser JavaScript syntax, etc. – will become perceived as less important relative to things that actually move the needle on performance, capabilities, etc.


Speaking as someone who works on the JavaScript spec - yes and no. I agree that terser syntax is less important (though I have thought this since before LLMs), and we should focus more on capabilities. On the other hand, I think it is now more important to have facilities for making code not just correct but obviously correct, and those largely fall into the "ergonomics" bucket.

Consider the new Disposable syntax for example - it's pure syntax sugar over try/finally, but harder to mess up. That's to the benefit of not-particularly-meticulous agents (and humans!) who are writing code, but even more so it is to the benefit of future readers of the code (human or otherwise). I could imagine an AI so meticulous that it could be trusted never to make mistakes even without such facilities, but we're not there yet.

Unfortunately it takes a very long time for any new language features to get into sufficiently widespread use for LLMs to start defaulting to them, so I don't know how much good this will do - it's an investment for 3-5 years in the future at best, and who knows what the world will look like then.

(Also JavaScript is kind of a special case because it doesn't really have capabilities as such, unless you count stuff like my base64 proposal. Anything that lets you do something genuinely new is defined elsewhere and worked on by a largely distinct set of people.)
